title: Effort as practice
hook: the fourth: joyful effort, not strain

segments.voice: Yesterday was patience, the third perfection: patience with people, with pain, with the truth. Did you get a chance to wait once, on purpose, without fighting the clock? Day one thousand four hundred two.

A young monk named Sona walks up and down a path in a forest grove, back and forth, hour after hour, so hard that his feet split and the path is marked with blood. He is pushing as hard as he knows how. And still his mind will not settle. Alone, he starts to think about quitting: going home, living as a lay person, spending his family's money on good things. The Buddha hears his thought and comes to him. He does not tell Sona to try harder. He does not tell him to give up. He asks him a question about music. Today is the fourth perfection, effort, and it starts with a sore pair of feet.
screen: `A MONK WALKING UNTIL HIS FEET BLEED.` → `READY TO QUIT.` → `A QUESTION ABOUT MUSIC.`

segments.voice: The question is this. Sona, before you left home, were you good at the lute? Yes, he was. When the strings were wound too tight, did the lute sound right? No. When they were too slack? No. And when they were tuned evenly, neither too tight nor too loose? Then it played well. In the same way, the Buddha says, effort pushed too hard turns into restlessness, and effort too slack turns into laziness. So tune your effort evenly. Sona does, and in the story he goes on to reach the goal he walked so hard for. That is the first turn of this perfection: effort is a tuning, not a maximum. The second turn comes from the Mahayana. In the list of six perfections a bodhisattva trains in, the fourth has a Sanskrit name, virya: energy, vigor. The poet-monk Shantideva, in his Way of the Bodhisattva, describes it not as grinding but as delight in what is good, taking pleasure in doing the wholesome thing. That is why some teachers call it joyful effort. Strain is effort that hates the work. Virya likes the work. The third turn is where the effort goes. The suttas name four right efforts: keep an unhelpful state from arising, let go of one that has arisen, bring up a helpful state that isn't there yet, and keep a helpful one going. All four are small and daily. None of them is a heroic all-nighter. So the fourth perfection is not about doing more. It is about doing the good thing gladly, at the right tension, and doing it again tomorrow.
screen: `SONA AND THE LUTE STRINGS.` · `NOT TOO TIGHT, NOT TOO LOOSE.` · `VIRYA: DELIGHT IN THE GOOD.` · then, large: `THE FOUR RIGHT EFFORTS.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, if you'd like, and let your hands rest. Notice your shoulders and your jaw. If they are tight, that is a string wound a little too far; let it ease a turn. If you feel heavy and dull, sit up a little taller; that is a string tightened a turn. Now choose one ordinary thing you will do after this: washing a cup, answering a message, a few minutes of work. Decide to do that one thing with glad effort, the way you'd play a song you like. Then come back to the breath, neither forcing it nor letting it go slack. The bell holds the time.
Effort as practice. Virya, the fourth perfection: energy that enjoys the good, tuned like a string, neither too tight nor too loose. Today's word.
Your line: the fourth perfection. Once today, when you catch yourself straining or dragging, ask the lute question: too tight, or too loose? Then tune it one turn. Day one thousand four hundred two.

howItsDone: Buddhists in the Mahayana schools count energy, virya, as the fourth of the six perfections; teachers in many schools use the Buddha's lute image from the story of Sona to describe balanced effort in meditation and daily life.

fork.setup: you're Sona. you've walked the path until your feet bled, and you're thinking of going home. what do you do?
options: go home and give up the robe.
tune your effort like a lute string.
fork.reveal: the Buddha's lute question turns him around: neither straining nor quitting, but even effort. in the story, it works.

original.note: Sanskrit virya (Pali viriya): energy, vigor; the fourth of the six perfections in the Mahayana list.

trapdoor: what you thought: effort means pushing as hard as you possibly can.
what it means: virya, energy tuned evenly, like a lute string, and glad to do the good.
what a scholar hears: the Buddha's advice to Sona in the Anguttara Nikaya, Shantideva's definition of virya as delight in the wholesome, and the four right efforts of the suttas.
